Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil (CNN) -- Former presidents of Mexico, Colombia and Brazil called Wednesday for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use and a change in tactics on the war on drugs, a Spanish news agency said. People march in support of legalized marijuana in late January in Belem, northern Brazil. Ex-presidents Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, Cesar Gaviria of Colombia and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil made their announcement at a meeting in Brazil of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, the EFE news agency said. "The problem is that current policies are based on prejudices and fears and not on results," Gaviria said at a news conference in which the commission's recommendations were presented. The 17-member panel worked on the report for a year and will forward it to all Latin American governments as well as the United States and the European Union, EFE said. Gaviria said the time is right to start a debate on the subject, particularly with the pragmatic openings provided by the election of President Barack Obama in the United States. "In many states in the United States, as is the case in California, they have begun to change federal policies with regard to tolerating marijuana for therapeutic purposes. And in Washington there's some consensus that the current policy is failing," EFE quotes Gaviria as saying. Decriminalization should be accompanied by treatment for addicts and public service campaigns on abuse prevention, the commission said. "If you don't help those who are dependent, you are half way there because they are going to commit crime to get money and pay for the drug," Gaviria said. Cardoso said the group called for only the decriminalization of marijuana and not other illicit drugs because "you have to start somewhere" and it would have been unrealistic to ask the same for all drugs, EFE said. Marijuana was chosen because it is grown in all countries in the region and because it is "less harmful." The decades-old criminalization of personal consumption has failed to stop the plant's cultivation and distribution, the group said. The commission urged that all current criminal prosecution be aimed at drug cartels and organized crime and not marijuana smokers, EFE said. Zedillo did not attend the news conference but worked on the report, Cardoso said. Wednesday's recommendation was the second time in less than a week that a Latin American government official called for decriminalization. A mayor in Peru suggested Friday that the federal government legalize illicit drugs and administer them through the national health ministry. Gusto Sierra, the mayor of the Surquillo district in Lima, said a federal drug law is hypocritical because it allows maximum legally allowed quantities for some drugs and plants but doesn't say where to acquire them, the Peru 21 newspaper reported in a front-page story headlined "Say yes to drugs?" Sierra said he will take the matter up with the nation's executive branch. Zedillo served as president of Mexico from 1994-2000. Gaviria was president of Colombia from 1990-94. And Cardoso led Brazil from 1995-2002.

People marched in support of marijuana legalization in late January in Belém, northern Brazil.

Former Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, former Colombian President César Gaviria, and former Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso issued their call during a meeting in Brazil of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, the EFE news agency reported.

The 17-member panel spent a year preparing the report and will send it to every Latin American government, as well as to the United States and the European Union, EFE said.

Gaviria said the time was right to begin a debate on the issue, particularly given the pragmatic opportunities created by the election of President Barack Obama in the United States.

“In many states in the United States, as is the case in California, they have begun to change federal policies with regard to tolerating marijuana for therapeutic purposes. And in Washington there’s some consensus that the current policy is failing,” EFE quoted Gaviria as saying.

The commission said decriminalization should be accompanied by treatment for people with addictions and public-service campaigns aimed at preventing abuse.

“If you don’t help those who are dependent, you are half way there because they are going to commit crime to get money and pay for the drug,” Gaviria said.

Marijuana was selected because it is grown in every country in the region and is considered “less harmful.” The group said that decades of criminalizing personal consumption had failed to stop the plant’s cultivation and distribution.

The commission urged authorities to direct criminal prosecutions toward drug cartels and organized crime rather than marijuana smokers, EFE said.

Sierra said he would raise the issue with the nation’s executive branch.

RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil (CNN) — Three former Latin American presidents on Wednesday urged governments to stop criminalizing marijuana possession for personal consumption and to rethink the broader strategy used in the war on drugs, according to the Spanish news agency EFE.

The proposal came from Mexico’s Ernesto Zedillo, Colombia’s Cesar Gaviria and Brazil’s Fernando Henrique Cardoso during a Brazilian meeting of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy. In late January, demonstrators in Belem, in northern Brazil, had marched in favor of legalizing marijuana.

Presenting the commission’s recommendations at a news conference, Gaviria said existing drug policies were driven by fear and prejudice rather than evidence of their effectiveness.

EFE reported that the commission’s 17 members spent a year preparing the document. The report will be sent to every government in Latin America, as well as to the United States and the European Union.

Gaviria argued that this was an appropriate moment to open a discussion, especially because President Barack Obama’s election had created opportunities for a more practical approach in the United States. He noted that states such as California had already begun moving away from federal policy by allowing marijuana to be used for medical purposes. He added that a degree of agreement had emerged in Washington that the existing strategy was not working.

The commission said removing criminal penalties should go hand in hand with addiction treatment and public-information campaigns intended to prevent drug abuse. Gaviria warned that reform would remain incomplete without assistance for people who are dependent on drugs, since they might commit crimes to obtain the money needed to buy them.

Cardoso explained that the panel was recommending decriminalization only for marijuana, not for other illegal substances. The group had to begin somewhere, he said, and seeking the same treatment for every drug would not have been realistic. Marijuana was selected because it is cultivated throughout the region and is considered less dangerous.

According to the commission, decades of making personal marijuana use a crime have not prevented the plant from being grown or distributed. The panel therefore recommended directing criminal prosecutions toward organized crime and drug cartels instead of people who smoke marijuana, EFE said.

Zedillo helped produce the report but was not present at the news conference, Cardoso said.

The announcement marked the second call for decriminalization by a Latin American government official in less than a week. The previous Friday, a Peruvian mayor proposed that the national government legalize illegal drugs and distribute them under the supervision of the country’s Health Ministry.

Gusto Sierra, mayor of Lima’s Surquillo district, described Peru’s federal drug legislation as hypocritical. He said it specifies the maximum legal quantities of certain drugs and plants that a person may possess but does not explain where those substances can legally be obtained. His comments appeared in a front-page Peru 21 article with the headline “Say yes to drugs?” Sierra said he intended to raise the issue with the country’s executive branch.

Zedillo was Mexico’s president from 1994 to 2000. Gaviria governed Colombia from 1990 to 1994, while Cardoso served as Brazil’s president from 1995 until 2002.

Former presidents Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, César Gaviria of Colombia, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil called on Latin American governments to decriminalize the possession of marijuana for personal use. Their proposal was based on a year-long review by the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, which examined the results of decades of prohibition and enforcement across the region.

The commission argued that existing drug-control policies have failed to reduce consumption or weaken organized crime. Instead, the “war on drugs” has contributed to violence, prison overcrowding, corruption, and the growth of powerful trafficking organizations. Campaigns built largely on fear and punishment, the panel said, have also done little to discourage young people from using drugs.

The former leaders stressed that decriminalization would not mean approving drug use or legalizing trafficking. Possession for personal consumption would no longer be treated primarily as a criminal offense, while production and large-scale distribution would remain subject to law-enforcement action. Governments would pair the change with stronger addiction-treatment services, honest public education, and prevention programs aimed especially at young people.

Marijuana was identified as the most practical starting point because it is considered less harmful than many other illegal drugs and is already widely cultivated and consumed. Reforming marijuana laws could allow police and courts to concentrate their resources on violent criminal networks and the trafficking of more dangerous substances.

The commission urged governments to treat drug dependence chiefly as a public-health issue rather than a matter for the criminal justice system. It also called for prevention campaigns grounded in scientific evidence instead of exaggerated warnings that can undermine public trust.

According to the panel, Latin America has borne a disproportionate share of the human and institutional costs of the global drug trade. The former presidents therefore called for an open debate, including a reassessment of policies promoted by the United States. They presented marijuana decriminalization not as a complete solution, but as a first step toward a more realistic, humane, and effective regional approach to drug control.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about former presidents of Mexico, Colombia, and Brazil calling for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use.
counterfactuals.output:
# Former Latin American presidents urge decriminalization of marijuana for personal use

**MEXICO CITY (CNN)** — Former presidents of Mexico, Colombia and Brazil have called for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use, arguing that decades of punitive drug policies have failed to curb consumption or weaken organized crime.

Mexico’s Vicente Fox, Colombia’s César Gaviria and Brazil’s Fernando Henrique Cardoso said governments should treat drug use primarily as a public health issue rather than a criminal offense. Their proposal would remove criminal penalties for adults who possess marijuana for personal consumption, while maintaining restrictions on trafficking and sales.

The former leaders said the region’s long-running “war on drugs” has contributed to violence, prison overcrowding and the growth of powerful criminal organizations without significantly reducing demand.

Decriminalization is not the same as full legalization. Under such an approach, possession of small amounts could lead to no penalty or to administrative measures, such as a fine or treatment referral, rather than arrest and imprisonment. Production and commercial distribution could remain illegal.

Supporters say the policy would allow police and courts to focus on violent traffickers while directing users toward prevention and treatment programs. Critics warn that easing penalties could normalize marijuana use and make drugs more accessible, particularly to young people.

The proposal reflects a broader debate across Latin America, where governments have borne much of the violence associated with the illegal drug trade. The former presidents urged the United States and other countries to reconsider policies centered on eradication, interdiction and incarceration.

Any change would require action by individual governments and legislatures, and drug laws vary widely across the region. Still, the intervention by three former heads of state adds political weight to calls for a new approach based on public health, education and harm reduction.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy’s recommendation to shift drug policy away from prosecuting marijuana users and toward combating cartels and treating addiction.
counterfactuals.output:
## Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy: A Policy Shift

In February 2009, the **Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy** called for a fundamental change in the region’s approach to illegal drugs. Its report, *Drugs and Democracy: Toward a Paradigm Shift*, argued that decades of “war on drugs” policies had failed to reduce consumption or trafficking while contributing to violence, prison overcrowding, corruption, and weakened democratic institutions.

The commission was led by former presidents **Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil, César Gaviria of Colombia, and Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico**, alongside other prominent Latin American figures.

### Principal recommendations

- **Decriminalize marijuana possession for personal use.** The commission urged governments to consider removing criminal penalties for cannabis users. This was not a blanket endorsement of an unrestricted commercial market; rather, it sought to stop treating users as criminals and to assess cannabis policy through evidence and public-health criteria.

- **Treat addiction as a public-health issue.** Governments should expand prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, and harm-reduction services instead of relying primarily on arrest and imprisonment. Drug users should be directed toward care when needed rather than pushed into the criminal-justice system.

- **Concentrate law enforcement on organized crime.** Police and judicial resources should target violent cartels, money laundering, arms trafficking, corruption, and the criminal networks that control production and distribution.

- **Use prevention strategies grounded in evidence.** The report favored candid education aimed particularly at young people, rejecting exaggerated anti-drug messages that can undermine government credibility.

- **Reconsider eradication-centered policies.** It argued that crop eradication and arrests of low-level participants often displaced production without dismantling trafficking organizations. Rural communities dependent on illicit crops should receive viable economic alternatives.

### Rationale

The commission concluded that criminalizing consumers absorbed resources that could be used against powerful trafficking groups. It also maintained that prohibition increased illicit-market profits, strengthening cartels and fueling violence—especially in Colombia, Mexico, Central America, and Brazil.

Its approach sought to distinguish among:

1. **Consumers**, who may need education or treatment;
2. **Dependent users**, who require health and social services; and
3. **Traffickers and violent criminal organizations**, who should remain the principal targets of enforcement.

### Significance

The report helped move Latin American drug-policy debate away from a predominantly punitive model and toward **decriminalization, public health, and targeted enforcement**. It did not advocate abandoning drug control altogether. Instead, it proposed reallocating state power: less prosecution of marijuana users and minor offenders, more treatment for addiction, and stronger action against cartels’ leadership, finances, weapons, and political influence.

The recommendations anticipated later reforms in several countries and contributed to broader international debate over cannabis regulation and the limits of prohibition.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed news story based on the 2009 meeting in Brazil where Ernesto Zedillo, César Gaviria, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso argued that the war on drugs was failing.
counterfactuals.output:
**Former Latin American Presidents Declare War on Drugs a Failure**

**RIO DE JANEIRO, Feb. 11, 2009** — Three former Latin American presidents called Wednesday for a fundamental change in international drug policy, arguing that decades of prohibition and aggressive law enforcement had failed to curb narcotics consumption while fueling organized crime, corruption and violence across the region.

Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, César Gaviria of Colombia and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil issued the warning as leaders of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, a panel of former officials, academics and public figures. At a meeting in Rio de Janeiro, the commission presented a report titled *Drugs and Democracy: Toward a Paradigm Shift*.

The report challenged one of the central assumptions behind the U.S.-backed “war on drugs”: that suppressing production and punishing users would eventually eliminate or sharply reduce the illegal market. Instead, the commission said, trafficking organizations had adapted, consumption remained substantial and the human costs had mounted.

“The war on drugs has failed,” Cardoso said in presenting the commission’s conclusions. The former presidents argued that governments should stop treating all drug consumption primarily as a criminal matter and instead place greater emphasis on public health, prevention and treatment.

Their recommendations included considering the decriminalization of marijuana possession for personal use, expanding treatment programs and concentrating police efforts on violent criminal organizations rather than low-level consumers. They also urged governments to conduct honest public education campaigns based on scientific evidence, rather than relying chiefly on fear of punishment.

The commission did not advocate the unrestricted legalization of all drugs. Its members drew a distinction between decriminalizing personal consumption—removing or reducing criminal penalties for users—and legalizing the production and commercial sale of narcotics. They said trafficking should remain subject to law-enforcement action, particularly when it involved violence, money laundering, weapons or corruption.

The intervention was striking because the three men had governed countries at the center of the hemisphere’s drug conflict.

Gaviria served as Colombia’s president from 1990 to 1994, when the country was confronting the Medellín and Cali cartels and enduring bombings, assassinations and attacks on state institutions. Zedillo governed Mexico from 1994 to 2000, as the country’s trafficking organizations grew more powerful and took on a larger role in transporting cocaine into the United States. Cardoso, Brazil’s president from 1995 to 2003, oversaw a nation with expanding domestic drug markets and heavily armed criminal groups operating in urban neighborhoods.

Their report argued that the policy of repression had produced a recurring “balloon effect”: pressure in one country or against one trafficking route displaced production and smuggling elsewhere instead of ending them. Operations that weakened one cartel often created room for another group to emerge.

The commission also said the burden of current policy had fallen disproportionately on Latin America. The United States and Europe supplied much of the demand, while countries to the south experienced the territorial battles, institutional corruption, prison overcrowding and killings associated with the illicit trade.

The report arrived at a particularly tense moment. Mexico was experiencing a dramatic escalation in drug-related violence following President Felipe Calderón’s decision to deploy the military against trafficking groups. Thousands of people had been killed in clashes among cartels and between gunmen and security forces. In Colombia, years of U.S.-supported eradication and interdiction had weakened some armed groups and altered coca cultivation patterns, but had not eliminated the cocaine trade.

Zedillo, Gaviria and Cardoso said those experiences demonstrated the need for an open debate free of ideological taboos. They called on the United States—the world’s largest market for illegal drugs—to review its approach and share responsibility for the consequences of demand within its borders.

The commission pointed to European harm-reduction programs and to Portugal’s decision to remove criminal penalties for possession of small amounts of drugs as examples deserving study. Such policies generally seek to reduce overdose deaths, disease and other damage without suggesting that drug use is harmless.

Opponents of decriminalization have long argued that easing penalties could normalize consumption, increase availability and weaken deterrence. The commission acknowledged that drugs carry serious health and social risks but maintained that punishment had often made those harms worse by driving users away from medical care and filling prisons with people who posed little threat to public safety.

Under the proposed shift, governments would reserve their strongest enforcement tools for traffickers, violent organizations and officials who facilitate the trade. Drug-dependent users would be directed toward health services, while prevention programs would focus on credible information and vulnerable communities.

The former presidents’ appeal did not immediately change national or international law. The United Nations drug-control system remained anchored in conventions requiring governments to restrict narcotics to medical and scientific purposes, and Washington continued to support interdiction, eradication and prosecution as major elements of its strategy.

Still, the Rio meeting marked an unusual break in the region’s political discourse. Rather than coming from activists or sitting leaders seeking a short-term policy change, the criticism came from former heads of state with direct experience managing the drug trade’s consequences.

Their central message was that the debate should no longer be framed as a choice between prohibition and surrender. The commission instead called for a combination of public-health measures, carefully considered changes to possession laws and more targeted action against violent criminal networks.

After decades of seizures, arrests and eradication campaigns, the former presidents said, success should be measured not by the number of people imprisoned or hectares of crops destroyed, but by whether policies reduce violence, addiction, corruption and the power of organized crime.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize Latin American leaders’ proposals to decriminalize marijuana, including their reasoning, relevant quotations, and the separate legalization proposal made by a Peruvian mayor.
counterfactuals.output:
Several Latin American leaders argued that marijuana prohibition had failed and that drug use should be treated more as a public-health issue than as a military or criminal one:

- **Guatemalan President Otto Pérez Molina** called for decriminalization—and potentially regulated drug markets—because the U.S.-led drug war had produced cartel violence without reducing demand. As he put it, **“The war we have been fighting for 40 years has not yielded results.”**
- **Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos** urged an open international discussion of alternatives, including marijuana legalization, while stressing that one country could not act effectively on its own. He said, **“If that means legalizing, and the world thinks that’s the solution, I will welcome it. I’m not against it.”**
- **Uruguayan President José Mujica** went further, backing government-controlled marijuana sales. His reasoning was that regulation would take customers and revenue away from traffickers and separate marijuana users from dealers selling harder drugs. Defending Uruguay’s willingness to experiment, he said, **“Somebody has to be first.”**

Separately, **a Peruvian mayor proposed outright legalization rather than simple decriminalization**: marijuana would be sold through licensed, regulated outlets, with controls on purchasers and taxation. The proposal was framed as a way to eliminate the illicit market, reduce dealers’ profits and violence, and allow the state to regulate consumption rather than merely punish users.

**Former Latin American presidents urge marijuana decriminalization, see opening under Obama**

RIO DE JANEIRO — Three former Latin American presidents are calling for the decriminalization of marijuana, arguing that decades of U.S.-backed drug policies have failed to reduce consumption while fueling organized crime, violence and prison overcrowding.

Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil, César Gaviria of Colombia and Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico say governments should treat marijuana use primarily as a public-health issue rather than a criminal offense. The former leaders, speaking through the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, also advocate prevention programs and treatment for drug dependence while maintaining firm action against violent trafficking organizations.

Their proposal would not legalize the drug trade. Instead, it would generally remove criminal penalties for possession of small amounts of marijuana for personal use, allowing police and courts to focus on major traffickers and more dangerous drugs.

The presidents say the region has paid a high price for the “war on drugs.” Colombia endured decades of cartel and guerrilla violence, while Mexico has faced increasingly bloody battles among trafficking groups and security forces. Across Latin America, they argue, aggressive enforcement has often displaced smuggling routes without substantially reducing demand in the United States and Europe.

Barack Obama’s election raised hopes among reform advocates that Washington might reconsider an approach centered on eradication, interdiction and prosecution. Obama entered office promising greater cooperation with Latin America and a less ideological foreign policy, encouraging expectations that the United States would be more willing to discuss prevention, treatment and demand reduction.

His administration’s early emphasis on shared responsibility — including recognition that U.S. drug consumption and weapons trafficking contribute to regional violence — also marked a change in tone from previous debates.

Still, supporters of reform acknowledge that a major shift is uncertain. Obama did not campaign on legalizing marijuana, and U.S. officials continued to back counternarcotics operations in Mexico, Colombia and elsewhere.

The former presidents say their immediate goal is to break a political taboo and encourage an evidence-based debate. After years in office enforcing prohibition, they argue that the current strategy has not achieved its central objectives and that governments must be willing to test alternatives.
